qs.q: A 28-year-old man suffers a displaced talar neck fracture following a high-velocity fall. He is counseled regarding a high risk of avascular necrosis of the talar body. Which vascular feature of the talus accounts for this risk?
o: Antegrade blood supply entering proximally at the posterior process
Retrograde blood supply entering distally and flowing proximally
Complete absence of capsular and ligamentous extraosseous flow
Total reliance on intra-articular synovial diffusion for nutrition
qs.e: The talus receives its predominant blood supply in a retrograde manner, with vessels entering distally at the tarsal canal and neck to supply the proximal body. Disruption of these distal vessels during a talar neck fracture deprives the proximal body of perfusion, whereas an antegrade flow would have spared it.
qs.s: Anatomy Spot Revision — Limb, Spine, Histology & Embryology —: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following anatomical features correctly describes the siding of a human talus bone using the table-top test?
o: With the inferior articular surface facing forward, the neck points lateral
With the lateral process pointing inward, the posterior tubercle faces down
With the rounded head pointing forward, the trochlear surface faces upward
With the trochlear surface facing downward, the head points directly back
qs.e: The talus can be sided using the table-top test where, with the rounded head pointing forward, the convex/concave trochlear surface faces upward. The talus is also unique in the foot as no muscles insert directly onto its body.
